stories.headline: House Shelves Hegseth Impeachment Push on 211-204 Vote
stories.dek: A procedural vote sent Rep. Thomas Massie's articles to committee, with 11 Democrats absent.
pole_a_bullets: Policy disputes over a war are not high crimes or misdemeanors, and impeachment should be reserved for real misconduct.
Many Republicans, including some who have clashed with Hegseth, say his conduct does not meet the impeachment bar.
The effort was a political spectacle, in Hegseth's words, and referring it to committee is ordinary House procedure.
Supporters point to military recruitment numbers and operations in Venezuela and Iran as evidence the department is succeeding.
pole_b_bullets: The articles describe serious abuses: starting a war without congressional approval, ignoring civilian-casualty rules, and ordering extrajudicial boat strikes.
Congress has a duty to check a defense secretary accused of these acts, and a procedural burial avoids that duty.
Democrats say the vote was lost through absences and should not have been close. Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove called the absences shameful.
Democrats note they take control of both chambers in January, so the issue can return.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions voiced by Hegseth, President Trump, Vice President Vance and House GOP leaders.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions voiced by House Democrats, Rep. Massie and progressive critics of the Iran war.
evidence_left: The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively killing it for the current Congress (CBS News, ABC News).
Rep. Massie was the only Republican to vote with all Democrats. Seven Republicans and 11 Democrats did not vote (CBS News).
evidence_right: The vote was procedural. It decided whether to send the articles to committee, not whether Hegseth should be impeached (Newsweek, ABC News).
Democrats who missed the vote included Nancy Pelosi, Julia Brownley and Frederica Wilson. Lou Correa disclosed a medical procedure (The Hill via Yahoo).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CBS News, ABC News, Newsweek, NBC News, November 11, 2026.

stories.headline: Hot October CPI Puts a December Fed Rate Hike in Focus
stories.dek: Consumer prices rose 0.4% as officials weigh a quarter-point or half-point move, and stocks rebounded Wednesday.
pole_a_bullets: One hot report does not settle the case for a half-point hike. One strategist called it a warning shot.
Falling gasoline prices gave consumers some relief in October.
Stocks bounced Wednesday, and the S&P 500 sat only about 4% below its record high after Tuesday's drop.
Markets are pricing in the hikes and the Fed is responding, which supports the case that inflation can be brought down.
pole_b_bullets: Core CPI rose 0.3% for a third straight month, roughly double the pace consistent with 2% inflation.
Inflation is eroding wage gains, which is why many voters rejected the party in power.
Fed officials are alarmed. Chicago Fed President Goolsbee called the report borderline disturbing, and Governor Waller floated a 50-basis-point hike.
Higher yields and hikes that may spill into 2027 threaten equity valuations and borrowers.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions voiced by market strategists and investors buying the dip.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions voiced by Fed officials, rate strategists and economists focused on persistent inflation.
evidence_left: Headline CPI rose 0.4% in October. The Latin Times reported a 0.3% consensus forecast, while The Hill cited a 0.2% Cleveland Fed projection.
Core CPI rose 0.3% against 0.2% expected (IBTimes). No year-over-year figure was published because of last year's government shutdown data gap (Kiplinger).
evidence_right: The Fed raised rates a quarter point in September, the first hike since July 2023. It held steady in October on a 10-2 vote (The Hill).

CME FedWatch showed a 100% chance of a hike after the December meeting, with 86.2% for 25 basis points (Benzinga). Stocks closed lower Tuesday (S&P 500 down 0.38% to 7,520.93) and rose Wednesday (CNBC).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CNBC, The Hill, Kiplinger, Benzinga, November 11, 2026.

stories.headline: Nvidia Board Probes CEO Jensen Huang's Ties to Alleged Chinese Spy
stories.dek: Shares fell two days, a shareholder suit was filed, and the stock rebounded Wednesday.
pole_a_bullets: Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.
Peers and chip stocks rallied through the scandal, so the damage looks specific to Nvidia, not to AI demand.
Huang remains CEO during the probe, and a Baird analyst downgrade still said the company will be fine.
Strong results from CoreWeave on Wednesday point to continued AI infrastructure demand.
pole_b_bullets: Key-person risk is large because Nvidia's AI ambitions are tied to Huang, as analysts have noted.
Huang and the company earlier called his dealings with Megaspeed normal, and a shareholder suit alleges investors were misled.
Governance questions remain open, including what the board knew and when, and a possible subpoena from House China committee leaders.
The scandal touches export controls and national security, which could bring regulatory and political fallout for the AI trade.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by bullish analysts and Nvidia's board.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by governance experts, securities lawyers and short sellers.
evidence_left: Huang told staff on Sunday he had been unfaithful. The board opened an independent investigation, and Wachtell, Lipton was retained (CNBC, The Hill).
Nvidia shares fell about 4.2% Monday (NBC News). Tuesday's drop was 5.47% per CNBC and roughly 5% per Yahoo Finance.
evidence_right: A class-action suit was filed in federal court in San Jose naming Nvidia and Huang (CNBC, The Hill). Shares rose roughly 5% Wednesday (Yahoo Finance).
The Information reported the relationship may have helped ship at least $7.5 billion of chips through Chinese firms. This was reported by Yahoo Finance and is not independently confirmed.
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CNBC, NBC News, The Hill, Yahoo Finance, November 11, 2026.

stories.headline: New York Opens RAISE Act Registration for Frontier AI Labs
stories.dek: OpenAI, Anthropic and other large developers must register by January 1, 2027.
pole_a_bullets: State-by-state rules create a patchwork that is costly to comply with and slows development.
Frontier AI policy belongs at the federal level, where one national framework can apply.
Incident-reporting deadlines and fines of up to $3 million add legal risk that could push research elsewhere.
Heavy state regulation can cede ground to global competitors, which is the concern behind industry calls for pacing and lighter rules.
pole_b_bullets: Voluntary self-regulation has not been enough. Gov. Hochul said the stakes are too high to take AI companies at their word.
Registration, published safety frameworks and 72-hour incident reports give regulators a view into the labs.
Independent evaluation through the new state AI research center adds technical expertise that the public lacks.
The federal government has not passed comprehensive AI law, so states are filling the gap, as California did with SB 53.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by AI industry groups and federal-preemption advocates.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by Gov. Kathy Hochul, state AI-safety advocates and consumer groups.
evidence_left: New York's DIGIT office opened the RAISE portal on Nov. 10. Large frontier developers must register by Jan. 1, 2027 (NY Governor's office, TechCrunch).
Covered developers are those with more than $500 million in annual revenue (IBTimes SG).
evidence_right: Critical safety incidents must be reported within 72 hours. Fines run up to $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for repeats (IBTimes SG, AI Weekly).
A New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research launched at Binghamton University, backed by $55 million in donations and capital. California's SB 53 took effect in January (TechCrunch).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from TechCrunch, NY Governor's Office, IBTimes Singapore, November 11, 2026.

stories.headline: Vikings Trade for Kirk Cousins as Raiders Hand Offense to Mendoza
stories.dek: Minnesota sent a 2027 third-round pick to Las Vegas after Carson Wentz struggled on Monday night.
pole_a_bullets: The Vikings got a proven starter for a third-round pick after their quarterback play hit a crisis point.
Cousins already knows coach Kevin O'Connell's offense, which cuts the learning curve for a 6-2 team.
He has produced this season, with 20 touchdowns and eight interceptions for the Raiders.
The Raiders also win by starting No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza and getting a pick for him.
pole_b_bullets: Minnesota is relying on a 38-year-old quarterback after one bad game from Wentz.
The Raiders were 4-5 and on the playoff bubble with Cousins, so moving him changes their season.
Starting Mendoza early moves up the timeline for a rookie and could stunt his development.
The Vikings' need was so obvious that Las Vegas could have held out for more, and reports say it first asked for a second-round pick.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by NFL analysts who gave both sides strong grades.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by skeptics of the Vikings' desperation and of the Raiders' rookie timeline.
evidence_left: Minnesota acquired Cousins for a 2027 third-round pick before Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET deadline (NFL.com, CBS Sports).
Cousins, 38, has 2,340 yards, 20 touchdowns and eight interceptions with the Raiders at 4-5 (NFL.com).
evidence_right: Wentz was 8-of-25 for 81 yards and two interceptions in Monday night's loss to Buffalo (Sports Illustrated).

NFL.com's Kevin Patra graded the trade A- for the Vikings and B+ for the Raiders (Yahoo Sports). Jordan Schultz reported the Raiders first sought a second-round pick; that report is unconfirmed (Yahoo Sports).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from NFL.com, CBS Sports, Sports Illustrated, Yahoo Sports, November 11, 2026.

stories.headline: Trump Calls Iran War 'Effectively Over' While Tehran Denies Talks
stories.dek: The US keeps its blockade in place and Iran rejects reports of negotiations.
pole_a_bullets: Iran's military has been destroyed, and the blockade and Task Force Iron Gate squeeze its economy without new strikes.
Pressure is working. Washington says Iran is talking, and mediators like Qatar are active.
Rubio calls Tehran's demands unacceptable, and a deal must address the nuclear program first.
Gulf neighbors favor keeping the status quo, which supports patience over escalation.
pole_b_bullets: Declaring the war over while the blockade, closed Hormuz and mine strikes continue is not an end to the conflict.
Tehran says no talks exist and that its seven conditions must be met, so claims of progress look hollow.
The war began without congressional authorization, which is a core charge in the Hegseth impeachment resolution.
Trump and Vance have tied the war's costs to Republican midterm losses, which suggests public support is thin.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions voiced by President Trump, Secretary of State Rubio and administration allies.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions voiced by Democratic lawmakers, war-powers critics and anti-war commentators.
evidence_left: Trump said Monday that Iran 'militarily, is effectively over' but kept the option of new strikes open. The status quo includes the naval blockade and Task Force Iron Gate (Euronews, Al Jazeera).
Rubio said Sunday that Iran's demands are unacceptable. CBS News reported he later said there is no need to restart combat operations.
evidence_right: Iran's Foreign Minister Araghchi denied any meeting was planned, and security chief Mohsen Rezaei rejected reports of talks (Euronews).
Brent crude fell to $92 a barrel Monday on hopes the war could end (Euronews). Iranian officials continue to press for the US to accept seven conditions (Al Jazeera).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from Euronews, Al Jazeera, CBS News, November 11, 2026.
